title: Hudson Enters the Harbor
text: Henry Hudson's Halve Maen enters the Upper Bay in September 1609. Forest covers Manhattan to the shore, and Lenape villages stand beside its creeks and ponds.

title: Lenape Manhattan
text: Bark-covered wigwams mark Werpoes above the Collect Pond, Rechtauck at Corlears Hook and the landing place Sapohanikan on the Hudson. The map draws them from Bolton's survey of Lenape sites.

title: Lenape Brooklyn
text: Marechkawick, the seat of the chieftaincy, stands near the East River shore, with villages at Werpos and Rinnegaconck close by. Woods and tidal marsh cover the rest of Kings County.

title: Manhattan Changes Hands
text: Director Peter Minuit acquires Manhattan from the Lenape for goods worth 60 guilders, as a letter of 5 November 1626 reports. The Dutch settlement rises at the island's southern tip.

title: Pavonia
text: A West India Company director buys the west bank of the North River from the Lenape - Hoboken, Ahasimus and Aressick - for a patroonship called Pavonia, opposite New Amsterdam.

title: New Haven Is Founded
text: Puritans led by John Davenport and Theophilus Eaton found the New Haven Colony in 1638 and lay the town out on a plan of nine squares around a central green.

title: Bronck's Land
text: Jonas Bronck settles on the mainland across the Harlem River in 1639; the river beside his farm, and later the borough, take his name.

title: Southampton
text: Settlers from Lynn, Massachusetts, found Southampton in 1640, an English town on the south shore of the eastern end of Long Island.

title: Southold
text: Puritans under the Reverend John Youngs settle Southold in 1640 on the north fork of Long Island, across Peconic Bay from Southampton.

title: Fort Amsterdam
text: Fort Amsterdam, begun in 1625, guards the southern tip of Manhattan; inside its walls stands the Church in the Fort, built in 1642. The Dutch West India Company's town grows around it.

title: Breuckelen
text: The village of Breuckelen on Long Island receives its own municipal government from the Dutch West India Company in 1646. It faces New Amsterdam across the East River, and farms and houses appear around it.

title: Esopus on the Hudson
text: Dutch farmers settle the Esopus flats on the Hudson in 1652; the village is later called Wiltwyck and becomes Kingston.

title: The Wall
text: In spring 1653 New Amsterdam builds a palisade across the island against an English attack, and houses fill the town behind it. The path along the wall becomes Wall Street.

title: Wyckoff House
text: The Pieter Claesen Wyckoff House in Flatlands dates from about 1652 and still stands, among the oldest surviving buildings in the state. Farmland of the Dutch towns of Kings County surrounds it.

title: New Amsterdam
text: Between the fort and the wall, the town's houses multiply along a few streets from 1656 to 1660. The Stadt Huys, a former tavern, has been the city hall since 1653.

title: Bergen
text: Stuyvesant orders a palisaded village laid out on the ridge behind Communipaw. Bergen, with its square and four gates, is the first permanent town in New Jersey.

title: Oude Dorp
text: Dutch and French-speaking families found Oude Dorp near South Beach, the first lasting European settlement on Staten Island; its first houses stand by 1664.

title: New Amsterdam Becomes New York
text: An English squadron under Richard Nicolls arrives at the end of August; Stuyvesant surrenders the town without a shot in early September and it is renamed for the Duke of York.

title: The Elizabethtown Purchase
text: Weeks after the English take New Netherland, men from Long Island buy the land between the Raritan and the Passaic from the Lenape. Elizabethtown becomes the first English town and the first capital of New Jersey.

title: Newark
text: Puritans from Milford, Branford and New Haven, led by Robert Treat, land on the Passaic and lay out a town along a broad street with a training place and a market place.

title: Conference House
text: The Billopp House stands on the southern tip of Staten Island, built about 1680. It later hosts the failed peace talks of 1776 between the British and a delegation of the Continental Congress.

title: The Counties
text: The Province of New York is divided into twelve counties, among them New York, Kings, Queens, Richmond and Westchester. Their boundaries still shape the five boroughs.

title: The Tappan Patent
text: Governor Dongan grants the valley of the Sparkill to sixteen Dutch families from Manhattan; Tappan becomes the seat of Orange County.

title: New Rochelle
text: Huguenot refugees settle on 6,000 acres that Jacob Leisler buys for them from John Pell, lord of Pelham Manor.

title: King's Bridge
text: A toll bridge owned by Frederick Philipse spans Spuyten Duyvil Creek, carrying the Boston Post Road from Manhattan to the mainland.

title: Philipsburg Manor
text: A royal charter makes Frederick Philipse lord of a manor that runs from Spuyten Duyvil to the Croton River, with tenant farms and mills at Yonkers and on the Pocantico.

title: Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow
text: A fieldstone church with a belfry is raised between 1685, the date on its bell, and 1697, when the congregation is organised, close to the mill of Philipsburg Manor.

title: Trinity Church
text: Trinity Church, built in 1698 at the head of Wall Street, serves the Church of England congregation of the English city. The palisade is down; its path remains as Wall Street.

title: The Revolt of 1712
text: On 6 April 1712 enslaved men set fire to a building near Maiden Lane and kill nine white colonists; twenty-one of the rebels are executed.

title: The Zenger Trial
text: John Peter Zenger, printer of the New-York Weekly Journal, is acquitted of seditious libel at City Hall on Wall Street, a landmark for freedom of the press.

title: Fire at Fort George
text: A fire in the governor's house inside Fort George in March 1741 begins months of panic over an alleged plot, and dozens of people are executed.

title: Connecticut Hall
text: Connecticut Hall, a brick Georgian dormitory finished in 1752 on Yale's Old Campus, is the oldest surviving building of the college.

title: Nassau Hall
text: Nassau Hall, finished in 1756 at Princeton, is the largest academic building in colonial America.

title: Sandy Hook Light
text: Sandy Hook Light, an octagonal stone tower 103 feet tall, is lit in June 1764 at the entrance to New York harbour and is the oldest working lighthouse in the United States.

title: The Stamp Act Congress
text: Delegates of nine colonies meet at City Hall on Wall Street in October 1765 and petition against the Stamp Act.

title: Morris-Jumel Mansion
text: Roger Morris builds this Palladian villa on Harlem Heights in 1765. In 1776 George Washington uses it as his headquarters during the fight for New York.

title: Golden Hill
text: On 19 January 1770 Sons of Liberty and British soldiers fight with swords and bayonets on Golden Hill by John Street, an early clash of the Revolution.

title: The King Falls at Bowling Green
text: On 9 July 1776 the Declaration is read to Washington's troops, and that night a crowd pulls down the statue of George III at Bowling Green.

title: Battle of Long Island
text: British and Hessian troops turn the American lines on the heights of Brooklyn in the largest battle of the war; Washington ferries his army to Manhattan two nights later.

title: The Night Retreat
text: On the night of 29 August 1776 Washington's army crosses the East River from Brooklyn to Manhattan in boats, under cover of fog.

title: Kip's Bay
text: On 15 September 1776 British ships bombard the shore at Kip's Bay and troops land; the Americans flee, and the British take Manhattan below the Heights.

title: Harlem Heights
text: On 16 September 1776 the Americans hold the British at Harlem Heights in a skirmish, their first success since the defeat on Long Island.

title: The Great Fire of 1776
text: Six days after the British take the city a fire starting near Whitehall Slip burns between 400 and 1,000 buildings, up to a quarter of the town, including Trinity Church.

title: Battle of White Plains
text: On 28 October 1776 British and Hessian troops drive Washington's army from Chatterton Hill at White Plains, and the Americans retreat north.

title: Fort Washington
text: On 16 November 1776 British and Hessian troops storm Fort Washington on the northern Manhattan heights and take nearly 3,000 prisoners.

title: Trenton
text: On 26 December 1776 Washington's army crosses the Delaware and defeats the Hessian garrison at Trenton. The Old Barracks of 1758 stand in the town.

title: Princeton
text: Washington defeats a British force at Princeton on 3 January 1777, and the British who remain surrender in Nassau Hall.

title: West Point
text: Colonel Rufus Putnam's 5th Massachusetts Regiment builds Fort Putnam in 1778 on the hill above West Point, to hold the Hudson Highlands.

title: Morristown
text: Washington's army winters near Morristown in 1779-80, and the general makes his headquarters in the Ford Mansion from December to June.

title: Evacuation Day
text: On 25 November 1783 the last British troops sail from the Battery, and Washington's army marches into the city.

title: Washington's Farewell
text: On 4 December 1783 Washington bids farewell to his officers at Fraunces Tavern on Pearl Street.

title: Capital of the United States
text: George Washington takes the oath of office at Federal Hall on Wall Street; New York is the national capital until 1790.

title: The Society for Useful Manufactures
text: Alexander Hamilton's Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures is chartered by New Jersey and chooses the Great Falls of the Passaic for a planned industrial city. Its raceways drive mills for 150 years.

title: Montauk Point Light
text: Montauk Point Light, an octagonal sandstone tower 80 feet tall, is begun in June 1796 and finished in November at the eastern tip of Long Island.

title: The Military Academy
text: President Jefferson signs the act founding the United States Military Academy at West Point on 16 March 1802.

title: The Town of Jersey
text: The Associates of the Jersey Company buy Paulus Hook and lay out a town opposite Manhattan, the beginning of Jersey City.

title: The Duel at Weehawken
text: On 11 July 1804 Aaron Burr shoots Alexander Hamilton in a duel on the Weehawken heights; Hamilton dies the next day in Manhattan.

title: The Commissioners' Plan
text: The commissioners' map fixes a grid of twelve avenues and 155 cross streets over Manhattan north of Houston Street. Above the town the island is still mostly farms and woods.

title: The Collect Is Filled
text: The Collect Pond, once the town's fresh water and by now polluted, is drained through a canal and filled; the Five Points slum rises on the sinking ground.

title: Steam Ferry to Brooklyn
text: Fulton's steam ferry Nassau begins crossing between Manhattan and Brooklyn, opening Brooklyn Heights to commuters.

title: The Erie Canal
text: The Erie Canal opens in 1825 and the canal boat Seneca Chief reaches New York nine days later. The canal makes the city the port of the interior, and South Street becomes its waterfront.

title: The Morris Canal
text: The canal from the Delaware reaches tidewater at Newark, lifting Lehigh coal over 23 inclined planes; it reaches Jersey City in 1836.

title: City of Brooklyn
text: The village and town of Brooklyn are incorporated as a city, soon the third largest in the country.

title: The Great Fire of 1835
text: In a freezing gale a fire burns seventeen blocks and between 530 and 700 buildings east of Broad Street, including the Merchants' Exchange.

title: The Erie Railroad at Piermont
text: The New York and Erie Railroad opens its first section, to Goshen, from the mile-long pier it built in the Tappan Zee, where passengers change to steamboats for the city.

title: Croton Water
text: The city celebrates the Croton Aqueduct, which brings river water 41 miles to a receiving reservoir in the future Central Park and a distributing reservoir at 42nd Street.

title: The Great Fire of 1845
text: On 19 July 1845 a fire and a saltpeter explosion destroy 345 buildings around Broad Street and kill thirty people.

title: Base Ball at the Elysian Fields
text: The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club plays the New York Nine on the pleasure grounds at Hoboken on 19 June 1846, the first recorded match under the Knickerbocker rules.

title: High Bridge
text: The aqueduct bridge that carries Croton water over the Harlem River is completed; it is the oldest bridge standing in the city.

title: The Astor Place Riot
text: On 10 May 1849 a riot over rival Shakespearean actors at the Astor Opera House ends when militia fire into the crowd; at least twenty-two die.

title: The Hudson River Railroad
text: Trains run from Manhattan up the east bank to Peekskill on a causeway that cuts off the river coves; the line reaches the Albany shore in 1851.

title: The Crystal Palace
text: The iron-and-glass hall of the Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations stands on Reservoir Square beside the Croton reservoir, with the Latting Observatory, a tall wooden tower, to its north.

title: Llewellyn Park
text: Llewellyn Haskell and the architect Alexander Jackson Davis lay out a gated residential park on the slope of Orange Mountain, the first planned garden suburb in the country.

title: Seneca Village Cleared
text: Seneca Village, a settlement of about 225 people founded by free Black landowners, and the other homes on the park site are cleared as construction of Central Park begins.

title: The Greensward Plan
text: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux win the Central Park design competition; the first section opens to skaters that December.

title: Lincoln at Cooper Union
text: On 27 February 1860 Abraham Lincoln speaks at Cooper Union against the spread of slavery, a speech that helps make him a presidential candidate.

title: Draft Week
text: In July 1863 violent disturbances shake Lower Manhattan, the culmination of working-class discontent with the new law drafting men to fight in the Civil War.

title: Navy Yard Through the Civil War
text: The Brooklyn Navy Yard fits out and repairs ships for the Union fleet, and its shops and storehouses multiply along the East River shore.

title: Garden City
text: The merchant Alexander T. Stewart buys 7,000 acres of the Hempstead Plains from the town and plans a town of his own with its own railroad.

title: Lyndhurst
text: Alexander Jackson Davis doubles the Gothic Revival house at Tarrytown in 1864-65 for George Merritt, adding a four-storey tower; it later belongs to Jay Gould.

title: The First Elevated
text: Charles T. Harvey's West Side and Yonkers Patent Railway demonstrates a cable-hauled elevated line above Greenwich Street; regular service begins in 1870.

title: The Orange Riot
text: On 12 July 1871 a clash over an Orangemen's parade on Eighth Avenue ends when militia fire into the crowd; more than sixty die.

title: Tweed Falls
text: Boss Tweed of Tammany Hall is arrested on 27 October 1871 after newspapers expose the frauds of his ring, among them the new county courthouse behind City Hall.

title: Yonkers Becomes a City
text: Yonkers is incorporated as a city in 1872, on the Hudson shore where Adriaen van der Donck's patroonship of 1646 once stood; two years later its southern part goes to New York City.

title: New York Crosses the Harlem
text: The city annexes the Westchester towns of Kingsbridge, West Farms and Morrisania, the western Bronx, in 1874; houses spread across their farms over the following years.

title: The Els Go Uptown
text: The Sixth Avenue elevated opens in 1878, followed by the Third Avenue line; steam trains reach Harlem by 1880 and open upper Manhattan to building.

title: Brooklyn Bridge
text: The East River bridge opens after fourteen years of work; its 1,595-foot span is the longest in the world.

title: The Dakota
text: The Dakota, designed by Henry Hardenbergh for Edward Clark, opens in 1884 on Central Park West, far from the built-up city.

title: Statue of Liberty
text: Liberty Enlightening the World is dedicated on Bedloe's Island in 1886, a gift of the people of France to the United States.

title: The Great Blizzard
text: The Great Blizzard of 12 March 1888 buries the city under up to 21 inches of snow and brings it to a halt.

title: Brooklyn Fills Kings County
text: Brooklyn, a city since 1834, spreads over the farms of Kings County. In 1894 it annexes Flatbush, Gravesend and New Utrecht, and Flatlands in 1896.

title: Carnegie Hall
text: Carnegie Hall has stood at Seventh Avenue and 57th Street since 1891; the model drawn here is the hall as enlarged in 1894-96.

title: Communipaw Terminal
text: The Central Railroad of New Jersey's Richardsonian Romanesque terminal has stood on Communipaw Bay since 1889; from 1892 it takes the trains of immigrants arriving from Ellis Island.

title: Poughkeepsie Railroad Bridge
text: The cantilever railroad bridge, 212 feet above the river and nearly 6,800 feet long with its approaches, has carried trains across the Hudson since 1 January 1889.

title: The World Building
text: The New York World Building on Park Row, 309 feet high, is the first building to rise above Trinity's spire. It stands until 1955.

title: Harlem River Ship Canal
text: The canal through the northern tip of Manhattan opens, cutting Marble Hill off from the island; eleven days earlier the city annexed the Bronx east of the Bronx River.

title: The First County Park
text: Essex County creates the first county park commission in the United States and takes over Newark's reservoir tract as Branch Brook Park.

title: Greater New York
text: New York, Brooklyn, western Queens County, Staten Island and the Bronx are consolidated into one city of five boroughs and 3.4 million people.

title: Nassau County
text: The three towns of Queens County left outside Greater New York - Hempstead, North Hempstead and Oyster Bay - become Nassau County, with its seat at Mineola.

title: Saving the Palisades
text: New York and New Jersey create the Palisades Interstate Park Commission, which buys out the quarries that are blasting the cliffs.

title: University Heights
text: The Bronx campus of New York University rises above the Harlem River, and the neighbourhood around it fills with houses. The domed Gould Memorial Library crowns it, with the colonnade of the Hall of Fame beside it.

title: Ellis Island
text: Ellis Island opened as an immigration station in 1892 and was enlarged with fill from about 3 to 27 acres; its main building is finished in 1900. Some twelve million people enter here by 1954.

title: Flatiron Building
text: The 22-story Fuller Building is completed on the triangle at 23rd Street, and is soon known by its shape.

title: Williamsburg Bridge
text: The second East River bridge opens with the longest suspension span in the world, 1,600 feet.

title: The General Slocum
text: On 15 June 1904 the excursion steamer General Slocum catches fire in the East River with a Lower East Side church party aboard; more than 1,000 die.

title: The Subway
text: The Interborough Rapid Transit opens from City Hall to 145th Street and Broadway, 9 miles and 28 stations.

title: Sagamore Hill
text: Theodore Roosevelt's house at Oyster Bay, built in 1885, gets its 40-by-30-foot North Room in 1905; it now has 23 rooms.

title: New Croton Dam
text: The New Croton Dam, begun in 1892, is finished in 1906: a masonry gravity dam 2,188 feet long and 297 feet from base to crest.

title: Hoboken Terminal
text: The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western opens its Beaux-Arts Hoboken Terminal in February 1907, with a clock tower 225 feet tall.

title: The Plaza
text: The Plaza, a hotel by Henry Hardenbergh in the style of a French chateau, opens in October 1907 at the southeast corner of Central Park.

title: Singer Tower
text: The 612-foot Singer Building becomes the world's tallest building in 1908, passed a year later by the 700-foot Metropolitan Life tower. The Singer is demolished in 1968.

title: Queensboro Bridge
text: The cantilever bridge over Blackwell's Island opens Queens to Manhattan; the Manhattan Bridge follows at the end of the year.

title: Harriman's Gift
text: Mary Averell Harriman gives 10,000 acres and a million dollars for a park in the Highlands on condition that the state give up the prison it is building at Bear Mountain.

title: Pennsylvania Station
text: The Pennsylvania Railroad opens its station by McKim, Mead & White with tunnels under the Hudson and East rivers. It stands until 1963.

title: The Triangle Fire
text: On 25 March 1911 a fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Company, on the upper floors of the Asch Building, kills 146 garment workers.

title: Titanic Survivors Land
text: On 18 April 1912 the liner Carpathia lands the survivors of the Titanic at Pier 54 on the Hudson.

title: The Armory Show
text: The International Exhibition of Modern Art opens on 17 February 1913 at the 69th Regiment Armory on Lexington Avenue and brings European modernism to America.

title: Grand Central Terminal
text: The new terminal opens over two levels of electrified tracks; the covered rail yard to the north becomes Park Avenue.

title: Kykuit
text: Kykuit, the Rockefeller house at Pocantico Hills designed by Delano and Aldrich, is completed in 1913 as a four-storey stone house of 40 rooms.

title: Woolworth Building
text: The 792-foot Woolworth Building opens, the tallest building in the world until 1930.

title: General Post Office
text: The General Post Office, by McKim, Mead & White, opens on Eighth Avenue opposite Pennsylvania Station on 5 September 1914. A hundred years later it becomes the Farley Building.

title: Port Newark
text: Newark opens a ship channel and docks dredged out of the meadows on Newark Bay; the Port Authority takes them over in 1948.

title: The Suffrage Parade
text: On 23 October 1915 some 25,000 women march up Fifth Avenue to demand the vote.

title: Black Tom
text: German agents blow up the munitions depot on Black Tom Island at the Lehigh Valley Railroad's piers. The blast breaks windows across Manhattan and scars the Statue of Liberty.

title: Hell Gate Bridge
text: The New York Connecting Railroad's steel arch, the longest in the world at 977 feet, opens between Queens and Wards Island.

title: Kingsbridge Armory
text: The Kingsbridge Armory, built from 1912 for the Eighth Coastal Artillery, is finished in the Bronx in 1917 with a drill hall over its whole footprint.

title: Oheka Castle
text: The banker Otto Kahn completes Oheka Castle on Long Island's North Shore in 1919: a 127-room chateau by Delano and Aldrich, with grounds by the Olmsted Brothers.

title: The Wall Street Bombing
text: On 16 September 1920 a wagon bomb explodes outside the Morgan bank at Wall and Broad streets and kills 38 people.

title: Harkness Tower
text: Harkness Tower rises 216 feet over Yale's Memorial Quadrangle, one foot for each year since the college's founding, and is completed in 1921.

title: Bear Mountain Bridge
text: The first road bridge across the Hudson south of Albany, briefly the longest suspension span in the world, opens on 27 November 1924 at the gate of the Highlands.

title: The Harlem Renaissance
text: Writers, musicians and artists, among them Langston Hughes and Duke Ellington, make Harlem the capital of Black America in the 1920s.

title: Bronx River Parkway
text: A landscaped motor road in a cleaned-up river valley opens from the Bronx to Kensico Dam, the first parkway of its kind. Westchester builds its other parkways on its model.

title: Lindbergh Takes Off
text: Charles Lindbergh lifts the Spirit of St. Louis off the muddy runway of Roosevelt Field on the Hempstead Plains on 20 May 1927 and lands in Paris 33 and a half hours later.

title: Coney Island
text: The Wonder Wheel (1920) and the Cyclone roller coaster (1927) stand beside the boardwalk and the beach, the amusement district of the Brooklyn shore.

title: Holland Tunnel
text: The first mechanically ventilated vehicle tunnel under the Hudson opens between Canal Street and Jersey City.

title: Staten Island's Bridges
text: The Goethals Bridge and the Outerbridge Crossing open to New Jersey, the first road bridges to Staten Island.

title: Newark Airport
text: Newark opens an airfield on filled meadow beside its port; through the 1930s it is the busiest commercial airport in the world.

title: Hutchinson River Parkway
text: The parkway is open from Pelham Manor to White Plains. Like the Saw Mill River Parkway, it follows a stream valley bought up as park land.

title: The Race for the Sky
text: 40 Wall Street and the Chrysler Building rise within months of each other. The Chrysler reaches 1,046 feet in 1930, and the Empire State Building will pass it a year later.

title: The Crash
text: On Black Thursday, 24 October 1929, panic selling begins at the New York Stock Exchange; the Great Crash follows within days.

title: Chrysler Building
text: The 1,046-foot Chrysler Building opens as the tallest building in the world.

title: Empire State Building
text: The 1,250-foot Empire State Building opens; it is the world's tallest building until 1970.

title: George Washington Bridge
text: The Hudson River bridge opens to traffic with a 3,500-foot span, nearly twice the previous record.

title: Bayonne Bridge
text: The longest steel arch in the world joins Bergen Point to Staten Island across the Kill Van Kull in November 1931.

title: Pulaski Skyway
text: A viaduct five and a half kilometres long carries the highway from the Holland Tunnel over the Hackensack and Passaic rivers and the meadows to Newark; it opens in November 1932.

title: Rockefeller Center
text: The RCA Building opens in 1933 at the centre of a complex of fourteen buildings built between 1930 and 1939.

title: The High Line
text: The High Line, an elevated freight railway on the Far West Side, is dedicated in June 1934 and runs from Spring Street up to 34th Street.

title: The Apollo
text: The theatre built on West 125th Street in 1914 reopens as the Apollo in January 1934 and becomes the stage of Harlem.

title: Triborough Bridge
text: Robert Moses's complex of three bridges joins Manhattan, the Bronx and Queens across Randalls and Wards islands.

title: The Hindenburg at Lakehurst
text: The airship Hindenburg burns while landing at Lakehurst on 6 May 1937. Hangar No. 1, built in 1921 for the Navy's airships, stands beside the field.

title: Lincoln Tunnel
text: The first tube opens between Weehawken and Midtown, its looping approach cut into the Palisades. A second tube follows in 1945 and a third in 1957.

title: Edison's Tower at Menlo Park
text: The 131-foot Edison Memorial Tower, topped by a glass bulb, is dedicated on 11 February 1938 on the site of Edison's Menlo Park laboratory; the map draws the tower, not the laboratory.

title: The Cloisters
text: The Cloisters opens in Fort Tryon Park in May 1938, a museum of medieval art built around cloisters brought from Europe.

title: The Merritt Parkway
text: The Merritt Parkway opens in 1938 from the New York line to Stratford and crosses the Housatonic River in 1940, a landscaped motor road through Connecticut's Fairfield County.

title: The World of Tomorrow
text: The World's Fair opens on Flushing Meadows, until then the Corona ash dumps, around the Trylon and Perisphere; the Bronx-Whitestone Bridge opened the day before.

title: LaGuardia Airport
text: New York Municipal Airport opens to airlines on filled land at North Beach in Queens.

title: Navy Yard at War
text: The Brooklyn Navy Yard builds and refits warships through the Second World War, and its shops, storehouses and slips multiply along the East River shore.

title: A Bomber in the Fog
text: On 28 July 1945 a B-25 bomber lost in fog strikes the 79th floor of the Empire State Building and kills fourteen people.

title: V-J Day
text: On 14 August 1945 crowds fill Times Square at the news of Japan's surrender.

title: Stuyvesant Town
text: Metropolitan Life's Stuyvesant Town rises over eighteen blocks of the Gas House District; the first tenants move in later in 1947.

title: Jackie Robinson at Ebbets Field
text: On 15 April 1947 Jackie Robinson plays first base for the Dodgers at Ebbets Field and breaks baseball's colour line.

title: Levittown
text: Levitt and Sons build rental houses on the potato fields of Island Trees from 1947; by 1951 there are 17,447, the model of the post-war suburb.

title: Fresh Kills
text: The city begins filling the tidal marsh of Fresh Kills on Staten Island with refuse; it grows into the largest landfill in the world before closing in March 2001.

title: Idlewild
text: New York International Airport opens on the marshes of Jamaica Bay; it is renamed for John F. Kennedy in December 1963.

title: Newark's Central Ward
text: Around Springfield and Belmont avenues, Newark's Central Ward is a dense district of houses, shops and churches.

title: Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel
text: The longest continuous underwater road tunnel in North America opens between the Battery and Red Hook.

title: New Jersey Turnpike
text: The toll road opens section by section from the Delaware; its northern end across the Newark and Hackensack meadows is finished in January 1952.

title: United Nations
text: The General Assembly Building opens beside the Secretariat (1950), completing the United Nations headquarters on eighteen acres of former slaughterhouses at Turtle Bay.

title: Garden State Parkway
text: The first toll section of the Garden State Parkway opens in Union County in January 1954; by 1957 it runs from Cape May to the New York line.

title: Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart
text: Newark's cathedral is dedicated on 19 October 1954, 56 years after ground was broken in 1898; its towers were cut from 332 to 232 feet in the redesign of 1913.

title: Last Train on Third Avenue
text: The Third Avenue elevated, the last in Manhattan, closes south of 149th Street and is pulled down.

title: Cross Bronx Expressway
text: The first sections of Robert Moses's expressway open. Cut through built-up neighbourhoods and displacing thousands of residents, the road is finished across the borough in 1963.

title: Tappan Zee Bridge
text: The New York Thruway crosses the Hudson at its widest point, between Nyack and Tarrytown, and opens Rockland County to the suburbs.

title: Ebbets Field
text: The Brooklyn Dodgers win the 1955 World Series, their first, and leave for Los Angeles after 1957. Ebbets Field in Crown Heights is demolished in 1960.

title: The First Container Ship
text: Malcom McLean's converted tanker Ideal X sails from Port Newark with 58 trailer boxes on deck. Within two decades the piers of Manhattan and Brooklyn stand empty.

title: Palisades Interstate Parkway
text: The parkway along the top of the cliffs is finished from the George Washington Bridge to Bear Mountain, on land John D. Rockefeller Jr. bought up and gave in 1933.

title: Lincoln Center
text: President Eisenhower breaks ground for Lincoln Center on the cleared blocks of San Juan Hill; Philharmonic Hall opens in September 1962.

title: TWA Flight Center
text: Eero Saarinen's TWA Flight Center, opened at Idlewild Airport in May 1962, has wings that sweep out over the apron.

title: Port Elizabeth
text: The Port Authority's Elizabeth terminal, opened in 1962 for Sea-Land, is the first facility built for container shipping; stacks of boxes fill the new ground beside Newark Bay.

title: Penn Station Demolished
text: Demolition of Pennsylvania Station begins; Madison Square Garden opens on the site in 1968.

title: The 1964 World's Fair
text: A second World's Fair opens at Flushing Meadows around the Unisphere, which still stands. Shea Stadium, home of the Mets, opens beside it the same year.

title: Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge
text: The bridge across the Narrows opens with the world's longest suspension span, 4,260 feet, tying Staten Island to the rest of the city.

title: Malcolm X
text: On 21 February 1965 Malcolm X is assassinated while speaking at the Audubon Ballroom in Washington Heights.

title: The Landmarks Law
text: Mayor Robert F. Wagner Jr. signs the law creating the Landmarks Preservation Commission, a response to losses like Penn Station.

title: The Beatles at Shea Stadium
text: On 15 August 1965 the Beatles play Shea Stadium in Queens to about 55,000 fans, among the first stadium rock concerts.

title: The Blackout of 1965
text: On 9 November 1965 a relay failure plunges New York and much of the Northeast into darkness for hours.

title: The Newark Uprising
text: Six days of unrest begin in Newark on 12 July 1967 after the arrest of a Black taxi driver; twenty-six people die.

title: Stonewall
text: On 28 June 1969 patrons resist a police raid on the Stonewall Inn in Greenwich Village, the start of days of protest that launch the gay liberation movement.

title: Woodstock
text: On 15 August 1969 the Woodstock festival opens on a dairy farm at Bethel in Sullivan County; about 400,000 people come over three days.

title: Co-op City
text: Co-op City rises in the northeast Bronx; the first residents move in during 1968. With 15,372 apartments it is the largest cooperative housing development in the world.

title: The Expressway Crosses Suffolk
text: The Long Island Expressway opens between Holbrook and Manorville in 1970, carrying the highway across central Suffolk County.

title: World Trade Center
text: The Port Authority dedicates the World Trade Center; the 110-story twin towers are briefly the tallest buildings in the world.

title: Newark After the Clearance
text: Between 1955 and 1975 the Newark Housing Authority clears much of the Central Ward, and after the 1967 uprising whole blocks stand empty.

title: The Fiscal Crisis
text: Despite large cutbacks and mass firings of city workers, New York almost defaults in October 1975. A Municipal Assistance Corporation and an Emergency Financial Control Board are formed to deal with the crisis.

title: The Blackout of 1977
text: On 13 July 1977 lightning strikes cut the city's power for about 25 hours; looting and arson sweep several neighbourhoods.

title: Battery Park City
text: The 92 acres of Battery Park City landfill, made partly from the World Trade Center excavation, are completed in the Hudson in 1976; the first apartments open in 1982.

title: The Meadowlands
text: Giants Stadium opens in 1976 beside the new racetrack on filled marsh at East Rutherford, the centrepiece of the state's plan for the Hackensack Meadowlands; the arena follows in 1981.

title: One Court Square
text: The Citicorp Building rises beside the Queens Plaza subway lines in Long Island City, a tower of the 1980s that becomes the tallest building in Queens.

title: The 1993 Bombing
text: On 26 February 1993 a truck bomb in the garage below the North Tower of the World Trade Center kills six people and injures more than a thousand.

title: Riverbank State Park
text: Riverbank State Park opens in May 1993: 28 acres of fields and courts on the roof of the North River sewage treatment plant, above the Hudson at 145th Street.

title: September 11
text: Hijacked airliners destroy the twin towers; most of the 2,977 victims of the day's attacks die here.

title: The Blackout of 2003
text: On 14 August 2003 a failure of the grid darkens New York and much of the Northeast and Ontario, about 50 million people.

title: The Miracle on the Hudson
text: On 15 January 2009 US Airways Flight 1549 glides to a landing in the Hudson River off Midtown after striking geese; all 155 aboard survive.

title: Yankee Stadium
text: The new Yankee Stadium opens in April 2009 across the street from the old one, which is demolished the following year.

title: The High Line
text: The first section of the park on the disused West Side freight viaduct opens between Gansevoort and 20th streets.

title: Occupy Wall Street
text: On 17 September 2011 protesters occupy Zuccotti Park near Wall Street and camp there until mid-November.

title: Barclays Center
text: The Barclays Center arena opens at the junction of Atlantic and Flatbush avenues in Brooklyn in September 2012.

title: Hurricane Sandy
text: A record storm tide of nearly 14 feet at the Battery floods the shores of all five boroughs, subway tunnels and the power network; more than forty people die in the city.

title: One World Trade Center
text: One World Trade Center opens at 1,776 feet, the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

title: The Oculus
text: Santiago Calatrava's Oculus, the transportation hub of the World Trade Center, opens in March 2016.

title: Second Avenue Subway
text: The first phase of the Second Avenue Subway opens with stations at 72nd, 86th and 96th streets.

title: A New Tappan Zee Bridge
text: The first span of the Governor Mario M. Cuomo Bridge opens beside the bridge of 1955, which is taken down by 2019.

title: Hudson Yards
text: Hudson Yards rises on a platform over the West Side rail yard; the first phase opens in March 2019.

title: The Spring of 2020
text: On 22 March 2020 a stay-at-home order takes effect as New York City becomes an early centre of the COVID-19 outbreak in the United States.

title: Moynihan Train Hall
text: Moynihan Train Hall opens on 1 January 2021 under skylights inside the old Post Office across Eighth Avenue from Penn Station.

title: The Brooklyn Tower
text: The Brooklyn Tower at 9 DeKalb Avenue, 325 metres to its crown, opens in 2022 above the Dime Savings Bank and becomes Brooklyn's tallest building.

title: The City Today
text: An estimated 8.58 million people live in the five boroughs in July 2025, down from 8.80 million in the 2020 census. The harbour Hudson entered in 1609 is still the centre of the city.
